title: Arguing from the inside
summary: Debate whether calculators belong in every math test, the same week you wired an adder yourself, then answer whether a calculator knows math.
materials: index cards or paper for the two sides

steps.title: You built the thing you are arguing about
steps.body:
This week's motion: calculators should be allowed in every math test. Most people argue about calculators from the outside, as a mystery box that spits out answers. You are no longer one of those people. This very week you wired the bottom cell of a calculator with your own hands, and you watched it match your paper truth table on every row.

Being on the inside arms both sides. For the motion: a calculator is not magic and not cheating, it is gates doing the boring part perfectly, which frees a person's head for the thinking part, the part no gate does. Against the motion: you know exactly how much a calculator does not do. It never decides what to add or why. And someone who cannot do the math themselves has no way to notice when the wrong question was typed in, so the machine's perfect answer to the wrong question sails right past them.

The steelman rule from last season still holds: before you argue your side, say the other side's best point so well that they would nod and say, yes, that is exactly what I mean. Then answer that point, not a weaker one.

And keep the question of the week in your pocket for the recording at the end: does a calculator know math? Your adder gets 1 plus 1 right every single time. Does it know that 1 plus 1 is 2, the way you know it? What is the difference?

steps.title: Build both sides
steps.body:
Make two cards, one for each side of the motion, before you know which side you will argue. On each card write a claim, one sentence you could actually say out loud, a reason why, and an example that makes it real. Pull your examples from your own bench this week: the adder that cannot miss, the truth table you wrote before the machine ever saw it, or the moment the screen agreed with your gates on every row.

Then pick whichever card feels harder to argue and practise its claim, reason, example out loud once. Arguing the harder side first is training with the weights on.
checklist: One claim, reason, example card for each side of the motion
Every example comes from something real on my bench or in my week
A steelman sentence for the other side is written down and sounds fair
I said the harder side out loud once before the debate

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record one round of the debate, or record yourself afterwards giving your strongest claim, reason and example. End the recording with your answer to the question of the week: does a calculator know math, and what is your reason?
